name: published-language
intent: Standardise the exchange between systems as one well-documented, versioned language - a schema or interchange specification that every participant translates to and from - so integration depends on a published contract instead of on each other's private model.
problem: Several systems, teams or organisations must exchange information, but no participant's internal model can be imposed on the others: every pair would need its own bespoke format and translator, each producer-side change would break each consumer differently, and a new participant has no artifact to read to learn the contract. The decision trigger is that the exchange format itself must be standard and documented - it has to live outside any one implementation so that unknown or future consumers can integrate against it.
context: Cross-team, cross-vendor or cross-industry integration that outlives a single deployment: industry and B2B interchange (iCalendar, vCard, HL7 FHIR, ISO 20022, EDIFACT), public APIs published to consumers you do not know, integration-oriented event schemas shared by many bounded contexts, and organisation-internal canonical schemas owned by a steering group. The language is usually carried by an Open Host Service; the format is owned by a standards body, consortium or the upstream team, while each participant keeps a translator (commonly inside an anti-corruption layer) between its own domain model and the published one.
benefits: Translator count falls from N x M to N + M: every participant maps only its own model to and from the published language, so six applications need twelve translators instead of thirty and a new participant adds one mapping rather than one per incumbent.

Third parties integrate from a document instead of private knowledge: the contract is a published schema plus prose, so an unknown or future consumer can build against it without access to the publisher's code or team.

The publisher's internal model stays free to change: refactoring classes, splitting services or replacing storage remains invisible as long as the same published language is emitted, which lets implementation and contract evolve at different speeds.

The published model can be deliberately restrained - an integration-only subset that exposes less than the internal model and hides complexity irrelevant to consumers - so the contract is smaller, more stable and easier to version than the domain itself.

One artifact drives several jobs: schema-first toolchains generate bindings and validators, produce documentation and examples, and give contract tests, mocks and code review a single source of truth.

Standards outlive implementations: an industry- or consortium-owned language (iCalendar, vCard, FHIR, ISO 20022) carries domain semantics and code lists that no single vendor would have the authority or the incentive to maintain alone.
tradeoffs: Governance is the price of admission: a standards body, steering committee or upstream team must own the language, review change requests and publish versions, and that institution costs time and politics before it produces any code.

The published model is a least common denominator: it can express only what the participants agree to document, so internal invariants, unit conventions and edge cases move outside the schema or get encoded in prose that validation cannot check.

Breaking changes become multi-party negotiations rather than a commit: evolution has to be additive, deprecations need windows measured in releases or years, and one poorly chosen field name can be frozen into the contract for a decade.

Every participant pays a permanent mapping tax: translators between the domain model and the published language are code nobody wants to own, and they must be maintained on both sides of every seam as long as the integration lives.

Validation gives structure, not meaning: a payload can satisfy the schema and still be semantically wrong (wrong currency, wrong code list, wrong unit), so schema conformance creates a false sense of correctness unless the semantics are documented and tested separately.

Adopting a language means adopting its toolchain: generators, runtime libraries and registry infrastructure must be kept on the standard's cadence, and generated bindings are a dependency the publisher cannot patch locally.

Version skew is permanent in the wild: unknown consumers, replayable logs and long-lived archives keep deprecated versions alive, so the publisher runs several versions concurrently instead of ever being finished.

participants.responsibility: The contract artifact itself: the schema or IDL, the media type or format definition, plus the prose that fixes meaning (units, code lists, invariants, examples), the versioning rules and the compatibility policy.

Owns and evolves the language: reviews change requests, decides what may be added or retired, publishes versions and deprecation windows - a standards body, a consortium, a domain steering committee or the upstream team.
Stores the versioned artifacts, assigns identifiers and disseminates them to participants, generators and validation tooling so that everyone validates against the same revision.
Per participant: converts the internal model into the published language on egress and back on ingress (usually inside an anti-corruption layer), keeping the domain model free of the exchange format.

Generated or derived language-native types, codecs and validators that make the contract executable in each participant's language; the place where schema changes turn into compile-time or validation errors.

use_cases: Industry and B2B interchange where a third party owns the vocabulary: calendaring (iCalendar), contacts (vCard), healthcare (HL7 FHIR), payments (ISO 20022), logistics (EDIFACT, GS1) - participants implement a standard they do not control.

Public APIs with unknown consumers: an OpenAPI description plus JSON Schema media types let clients generate their own bindings and validate responses, while the provider evolves the implementation behind a stable contract.
Integration-oriented events between bounded contexts: the organisation publishes the event schema downstream contexts consume as public events and keeps internal domain events private.
Platform and plugin ecosystems: a host system publishes the file or wire format its extensions and partners must speak - document formats, package manifests, media types.
Polyglot service estates: one protobuf or IDL contract with generated bindings per language, so no team hand-writes a serialiser per language pair.
Long-lived archives and replays: records written today must be readable years later, so the schema is versioned with the data and every reader validates against the version the record declares.

Healthcare interoperability with HL7 FHIR: resource definitions, formats and a published version directory let hospitals and vendors implement the same exchange language while each maps local clinical models at its boundary.

Cross-border and domestic payments with ISO 20022: the governed message repository and metamodel give banks and payment systems a shared, versioned vocabulary while participants retain local processing models.

Public HTTP APIs with OpenAPI: a machine- and human-readable description gives unknown consumers a stable, language-neutral contract for generated clients, documentation and validation without exposing the provider's implementation.
avoid_when: Only two systems you control and can deploy together need to talk: a direct Message Translator or a shared library is cheaper than standing up a governed standard.
The integration is a throwaway or a one-off migration: publish a schema only when a consumer you cannot see, or a lifetime beyond the next release, justifies it.
Both sides really share one model (a single bounded context, or a deliberately shared kernel): sharing the model is the honest simplification, not translating between dialects of one language.

Nobody can say no to changes: without a steward who rejects additions and enforces a compatibility policy, the published language drifts into per-consumer dialects within a few releases - use a conformist relationship or an anti-corruption layer instead.
The hot path cannot afford an external standard's overhead or its flattened shape: an internal, documented binary format with a private schema is the better trade.
The information is internal to one context: publishing it as a language invites coupling - keep it a private event, a method call or a local module API.
anti_patterns: Publishing your internal domain model as the language: consumers couple to implementation details, and every refactoring becomes a breaking change for people you cannot see.
'Published' in name only: no schema artifact, no version, no compatibility policy, no owner - the format exists only as one team's code and dies with it.
Per-consumer dialects: the steward cannot say no, so each consumer gets a special field or extension and the standard fragments until every integration is bespoke again.
Hand-edited bindings drifting from the schema - generated code patched in place, or validation quietly disabled in production, so artifact and running system disagree.
Treating schema validation as correctness: no semantics documented, no code-list checks, no contract tests - payloads validate and integrations still fail.
Big-bang versioning: replacing the language wholesale (v2 is a new format) instead of adding optionally and retiring deliberately, forcing every unknown consumer to migrate at once.
design_principles: Publish an explicit contract; never let the exchange format be inferred from one implementation's behaviour.
Depend on the published abstraction, not on the other participant's model: translation points inwards, which is dependency inversion at the boundary.
Separation of concerns: translation is a boundary responsibility, not domain logic - the domain model stays free of wire shapes.
Least knowledge and information hiding: expose the restrained integration subset, not the internals - a published language is a facade over the context.
Stability through single ownership: one steward owns additions, compatibility and deprecation, so a shared contract cannot drift per consumer.
Open/closed at the ecosystem level: new participants integrate without modifying the language or the existing participants.
best_practices: Write the schema plus the prose that fixes semantics (units, code lists, invariants, examples per version) and give the language a name, a version identifier and an owner before the first consumer integrates.
Prefer an existing industry standard or widely used media type over a bespoke schema whenever one covers the domain, and extend it only in the way that standard allows.

Design for additive evolution: optional fields, reserved names and numbers that are never reused, explicit defaults, and a documented policy for unknown fields (producer: never renumber; consumer: ignore what you do not need).
Generate bindings and validators from the single schema artifact and keep regeneration in the build - never hand-edit generated code - so schema changes surface as compile-time or validation errors.

Version and distribute artifacts through a registry with identifiers and checksums, and validate at the boundary, routing invalid payloads to an invalid-message or dead-letter path instead of dropping them.
Document deprecation windows and keep several versions readable at once, because stored payloads and unknown consumers outlive any migration timeline.
Pin the contract with consumer-driven contract tests and schema-compatibility checks in CI, so a producer-side change is rejected before it reaches other participants.
sources: Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (2003) - Published Language (Chapter 14, Maintaining Model Integrity; p. 330): 'Use a well-documented shared language that can express the necessary domain information as a common medium of communication, translating as necessary into and out of that language.'
https://www.domainlanguage.com/ddd/reference/ (Evans, DDD Reference - Published Language: many industries establish published languages in the form of data interchange standards).
https://github.com/ddd-crew/context-mapping (Context Mapping cheat sheet - Published Language, with iCalendar and vCard as widely known examples; often combined with an Open Host Service).
https://pubs.opengroup.org/architecture/o-aa-standard/DDD-strategic-patterns.html#_midway_patterns (Open Group O-AA Standard, DDD strategic patterns - Midway patterns: Published Language).

https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/CanonicalDataModel.html (Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns - Canonical Data Model, the messaging-catalogue sibling: N*M translators collapse to N+M).

Khononov, Learning Domain-Driven Design (2021), ch. 3 and 15 - the published language as an integration-oriented language: public versus private events, a deliberately restrained model, and scope limited to its own bounded context (unlike a canonical data model).

https://www.domainlanguage.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/DDD_Reference_2015-03.pdf (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design Reference: Published Language is a named DDD strategic pattern and published data interchange standards are examples).
https://hl7.org/fhir/overview.html (HL7 FHIR R5 official overview: a published specification for interoperable healthcare data exchange with resource definitions, formats and versioned directories).
https://www.iso20022.org/iso-20022 (ISO 20022 official overview: an international standard and repository for common financial messages, with maintenance processes).
https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html (OpenAPI Specification: language-agnostic, machine- and human-readable HTTP API contract supporting client generation and discovery).

https://pactflow.io/blog/schemas-can-be-contracts/ (PactFlow Drift critique: schemas alone do not guarantee runtime behavior or capture undocumented consumer dependencies; pair specification checks with contract testing).
